title: Why do humans have body hair?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore why humans have body hair. They open with casual banter about shaving and puberty, then explain the hair growth cycle (anagen and telogen phases), the types of hair (lanugo, vellus, terminal, androgenic), and the fact that humans and chimps have similar follicle density but differ in hair size. They cover evolutionary theories: losing hair after becoming bipeds and sun exposure, the water-dwelling ape idea, and moving from forest to savannah around 1.7 million years ago. They then discuss skin pigment (MC1R gene) research by Dr. Rosalind Harding of Oxford, suggesting hairlessness for at least 1.2 million years. Next comes hypertrichosis, the Gomez family ("wolf people") and Xin Juan, the hairiest man in China, plus acquired forms from malnutrition. The episode closes with a hypothesis that underarm and genital hair acts as a pheromone amplifier, a blog plug, and a correction segment about the cane toad episode, HPV pronunciation, and other errata.

segments.title: Opening banter and shaving memories
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the episode with a sponsor line, then chat about recording on a Monday, childhood shaving, and late puberty and facial hair.

segments.title: How hair grows and hair types
segments.summary: The hosts explain follicle cell division, keratin, and the anagen and telogen growth and resting phases. They then cover lanugo, vellus, and terminal hair, and androgenic hair driven by testosterone.

segments.title: Humans versus chimpanzees hair density
segments.summary: Average adults have about five million follicles, roughly the same density as chimps. Human hair is finer and shorter, and humans and chimps share hairless lips, palms, and soles.

segments.title: Evolutionary theories for body hair loss
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the bipedalism and sun exposure theory, the aquatic ape idea supported by hairless water mammals, and the forest-to-savannah move about 1.7 million years ago with its temperature argument.

segments.title: Skin pigment and the MC1R gene
segments.summary: Skin pigment is presented as the replacement for hair as UV protection. Rosalind Harding of Oxford traced MC1R gene mutations and found a sweep about 1.2 million years ago, suggesting humans have been largely hairless since then.

segments.title: Hypertrichosis and the hairy families
segments.summary: The hosts describe hypertrichosis, the Ramos Gomez family of nineteen across five generations, and Xin Juan, the hairiest man in China. They also note acquired hypertrichosis from malnutrition and the usual hair-removal options.

segments.title: Underarm and pubic hair as pheromone amplifiers
segments.summary: Josh asks why underarm and genital hair grows. The hypothesis is that these pheromone-producing areas have hair that traps and amplifies smell. Christen Conger's article on the topic is mentioned.

segments.title: Blog plug and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts plug their blog and the Goodness Round Up podcast and then say goodbye.

segments.title: Listener mail corrections
segments.summary: Corrections include the cane toad predator and Perth detail, HPV pronunciation, the crocodile versus alligator mix-up, salicylic acid pronunciation, the Ocala and Wisconsin pronunciation, and listener tips on removing warts.
